title: Valid Reasons to stop divulging your game is made with AI.
author: 3xNEI

comments.body:

replies.body: I definitely wouldn't lie / *forget* to disclose on steam. The instant player discover a proof - and they will - you'd be liable for zero-conditions refunds (at best)

replies.author: Total_Engineering_51
replies.body: Only for art and other user facing elements—RT AI integration cases, marketing materials and so on. Use of it for coding has no disclosure requirement. Few care as long as the game code runs well and Valve realizes this… not to mention they are likely using AI for code themselves and don’t want to open that can on themselves.

replies.author: Rand0m7
replies.body: Appreciate the clarification! Been slowly working on a a.i game myself

replies.author: Ok-Foundation-8006
replies.body: Would a procedural engine that creates characters or environment be considered AI art and need to be disclosed? Ex. A creature generator where the code defines various parts, sizes, and taxonomies and assembles them. Genuinely curious as art has many different forms, some consider their code to be “art”.

replies.author: Mundane_Background19
replies.body: You are referencing the use of scripted code and do not have an LLM in the loop, so this is proc gen.

replies.author: Ok-Foundation-8006
replies.body: Does that change if AI was used to help create such an engine? For added clarity every part would be literal code, and not be pre generated by AI using tools like Meshy etc…

replies.author: Mundane_Background19
replies.body: Think of it this way.. you’re asking an AI to write code for you. It doesn’t matter where the code sits. It’s the behavior. The code isn’t calling an LLM so while it will vary wildly in its output, it won’t vary infinitely like an LLM in the loop would. You can govern the proc gen code so it’s not AI art.

replies.author: Ok-Foundation-8006
replies.body: Thanks for the clarifications boss, greatly appreciated! 🙏

replies.author: Tyalou
replies.body:
The problem with AI in games has never been that LLM are in the loop of the game (very few games really do that). The problem is that an LLM was used to build art, your analogy to the code is like saying since the 3D AI generated model doesn't need an LLM to run, it's not AI... Well sure, but it surely was generated with AI.
Now, usually code is not as descriminated as Art so this will hit people differently.

replies.author: Mundane_Background19
replies.body: I think you may be misinterpreting what Ok-Foundation is asking. In their work stream, they are working with AI to develop something like a procedural combinatory or generation product. I don’t see anywhere where they are promoting the LLM for artwork.

replies.author: Tyalou
replies.body: They are saying they used AI to generate a code that does procedural generation. The procedural generation is not AI, the code was created with AI. See their follow-up post.

replies.author: Mundane_Background19
replies.body: Thank you for proving my point.

replies.author: Tyalou
replies.body: I was making an analogy.

replies.author: Ok-Foundation-8006
replies.body:
I’ll disclose AI was used for coding, it was more specific to whether or not it constitutes as ‘Art’. For context I have used AI generated images as references but it was more a way to provide context for parts. Ex. This is what a bat wing looks like instead of saying “add wings” lol. The generations look nothing like the references and even then I imagine using references are a standard part of any creative endeavour as long it’s not plagiarizing.

I went down a rabbit hole after this through steamdb and was surprised to see many popular games disclose their use of AI similar to what I’ve described.

replies.author: Overall-Muscle5313
replies.body:
I'd argue this doesn't hit people at all, when it comes to code, as disclosure of code is not necessary.

So unless someone fully decompiles a game and checks the base code, there's no way for people to tell this.

As opposed to art, which is customer facing, and which is required to be disclosed under Steam rules.

Might also be wrong but I don't think other vendors have stricter rules than Steam

replies.author: Tyalou
replies.body: Sure, I'm just saying most AI haters don't want AI in their game, not just Art, they reject AI in mass. Sure you can not reveal it (though now any Claude code line will be traceable) but AI was used and not revealing is a bit like not revealing you used it for art. I don't know, the whole debate is a bit stale but it's really hard to know where to stand.

replies.author: Overall-Muscle5313
replies.body:
Regarding Claude, they did that to comply with an EU regulation. So it is very likely everyone else will follow suite soon enough.

Regarding disclosing AI code vs AI art, as long as Steam clearly says AI code is not the same as AI art, why would you or I make that assumption? So I strongly disagree that it is a bit like not revealing AI used for art - it's like comparing apples and oranges.

I think the only people that care for AI code disclosure are the anti AI luddites, because as you mention they just hate AI as a whole.

replies.author: Tyalou
replies.body: Isn't that disclosure exactly for that crowd? So the only one who care about art would also care about code. No?

replies.author: SBC_packers
replies.body: So all of my art is generated by an LLM using blender MCP and doing hundreds of iterations to get it as close to my input images as possible but what it returns to me in the end is a blender script as a recipe to generate that asset locally. All it's doing is writing code and checking quality. I'd still consider it AI art. Also i don't think it matters at all. By the time I release something people will have put down the pitchforks.

replies.author: Turbulent-Armadillo9
replies.body: Right. I’m almost certain every AAA studio uses ai in some way or another.

replies.author: Tyalou
replies.body: Not using AI nowadays is almost like not using a computer, all the AI features jump at you and before you know it you made 5 LLM queries.

replies.author: fatheadlifter
replies.body:
Every single enterprise/engineering staff at every company is either evaluating AI use or using it.  At a minimum it's a useful tool for writing documentation, which nobody wants to do.  At a minimum it's useful for code porting and cleanup.

Yes it can do these things, if you guide it and use it right, and have the right level of complexity to give it.  Which will be most tasks most of the time.

replies.author: RevenueChemical6910
replies.body:
\> Use of it for coding has no disclosure requirement.

This distinction between "AI is okay for coding" and "AI is not okay for art" is kind of dumb

replies.author: Tight_Principle9572
replies.body: Genuine question. What happens if they say no it wasn't made with ai and it is? Can the system detect it?

replies.author: Total_Engineering_51
replies.body: Not as such, not up front anyway. They aren’t scanning and are instead leaving it to devs to disclose. Once they have creditable reports of suspected usage without disclosure, then they might start looking for specific tells and such but I’m not sure. The enforcement side is pretty murky at this point, so it’s hard to point and say, “don’t do this” definitively. That’s likely two parts by design to limit circumvention and one part as a hedge against all the uncertainty around everything right now, basically allowing them to move the goalposts behind the scenes.

replies.author: Tight_Principle9572

replies.author: Alive-Shoulder-4042
replies.body:
No one should feel entitled to unconditional honesty.

Honesty is commonly lost if you make people uncomfortable, or it otherwise negatively impacts them. 

I’m pro-choice. I’m not ashamed of being pro-choice but I’m not going to put a pro-choice bumper sticker on my car because someone will feel it’s their moral right to key my car over it.

I’m also not going to give someone my credit card info even if they ask nicely.

Steam hasn't unlisted titles outed for using GenAI undisclosed, because at the end of the day steam also just wants to make money and their systems already screened out bad games.

comments.author: Dumpfumpkin
comments.body: I’m choosing to be transparent because while I disagree with the anti-AI sentiment I can appreciate that some people view their opposition to it as a matter of ethics or morality, and I don’t want to infringe on those beliefs. I think of it kind of like serving food to a vegan: I’m making a dish with meat, and I have an ethical obligation to make sure it doesn’t end up on their plate.

replies.body: That's actually a pretty good argument.

replies.author: whimsicaljess
replies.body:
it's not, actually. 

for example, some people think it's a matter of ethics or morality that LGBT people should not be allowed to live, but the _objectively correct_ answer here is the classically liberal one ("their own personal lives are not your business, it is not up to you what consenting adults do in their own lives").

"i don't want to infringe on sincerely held beliefs" is the kind of thing that sounds deep but is actually braindead.

replies.author: platypus-3fh98hhwefd

irrelevant because neither of those are ethical concerns to a large subset of customers (regardless of if you personally disagree), nor copyright/liability concerns on the platform's side

If you believe you should be free to use whatever tools you want for development, it would be hypocritical to be against giving customers the ability to make *relevant* informed choices. In a commercial project, just because you disagree with someone's ethics doesn't mean you're right for wanting to trick them out of their money

replies.author: Kuben_I_Blisk
replies.body:
I don't see how this compares since no one considers your power usage a ethical concern, hypothetically how would one even measure that even on the smallest single man Indie build team? Let alone the 100 or 1000 person teams developing games.   
In the case of AI for most people its not a how much its a Yes or No. Which is both simple and measurable, did I use it, Yes, or did I not, No.   
Circle back to the power thing, if anyone actually did have that concern, whats considered too much? Lets frame it with Vegans, Any animal product is too much (Or in this case any power) Well then I think your not even in the range they are marketing too, then you have vegetarians who all have ranges, some allow milk but not eggs, some allow both, how does one decide what is too much power and why? Clearly anyone who has this concern has to trust the game devs measurement is both accurate and not a lie but any kind of game company more then 1 person would use too much so clearly I think they just wouldn't game ever

comments.author: sessamekesh
comments.body:
The "it's just a tool" argument is a good one, but copy-pasting Romeo and Juliet with a find/replace is "just using a tool" too. Tracing existing art is "just using a tool".

Consumers care, some of the reasons they care are good ones and some of them are bad. Is your goal to build something for others to play or is it to stroke your own ego? Hiding AI detail isn't bad if you are making a game intended for people to enjoy and play, and if that isn't your goal I don't really give two shits how you feel about disclosure on consumer-friendly platforms.

*Overwhelmingly* I find that the people who peddle the "luddites just hate progress" are the worst offenders when it comes to AI slop. I've never had an issue being frank and transparent about my AI usage even in *exceptionally* anti-AI spaces. There are proper luddites but they make up such a small portion of people that I don't even bother listening to them.

comments.author: EternalPump
comments.body:
Look, I've seen a lot of these posts so I'm going to choose to respond to this one.

AI has a morality problem because of how it was produced. This isn't a debate - it's a well established fact that many forms of AI today were bootstrapped with non-consensual content. Some people don't want to support that. The disclosure of AI is about giving users the right to be informed in making their financial choices and supporting certain types of people; such as people who don't use things bootstrapped in ways they find morally objectionable. That's a "pro-consumer" sentiment, which, hey you can choose to be "anti-consumer" and that is a reason people shouldn't support your products.

If you use the thing built on unethically taking tons of other people's work without their consent, because it makes your life easier, then you need to accept some people are going to hate you for it. That's the price you pay for being able to work 10x faster. Using the thing built on pirated (not stolen) work, and then using arguments as to why people shouldn't be allowed to know you used it because you don't want to suffer the consequences of that unethical exploitation is just a bad look man. It kind of reinforces that people should be cracking down harder on disclosure requirements, because people like you are more concerned about decieving your players so you can have an easier time than giving them an informed choice.

Are people freaking out over banal use of AI? Yes. But when we choose to use it, we accept the risks. If you want to change users minds, then work towards that, but don't lie to them.

replies.author: platypus-3fh98hhwefd
replies.body:
And of course this sort of opinion is either rare or downvoted among pro-ai communities

Honesty and informed consent (both for training data and for consumers) are fine until they get in the way of "progress", apparently

replies.author: EternalPump
replies.body: Yes, it's quite concerning how common this sentiment is.

comments.author: brendonx
comments.body:
I’ll preface my response by saying I have no problem with AI and would love to see the open source locally run AI tools become good enough to replace the big players. 
 I feel like the difference between other tools and AI is the perception, and likely the reality, that it was trained illegally on data that was taken from everybody. Everybody with an online presence was bundled up and used to train these things. Conversations you thought were relatively private, your GitHub repository, art, music, etc were taken and in the earlier days without asking, informing, or even giving the chance to remove your content from sites prior to this, and a competitor was trained from it. 
In fact, now that I write it out, it seems obvious. You should disclose it because people should be allowed to make an informed decision. Like if people found out Jeffrey Epstein made a new movie I imagine there would be a decent number of people who would want to avoid it, and they should have that right. 
It’s not other people’s problem that you choose to use a tool they don’t like. It’s your problem, and for clarity’s sake when I say your problem I’m not insinuating you’re bad for using it, I’m saying it’s your obstacle to overcome.
